16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Devin CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Devin CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Devin CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives and leveraging Devin's multi-model surface, subagent delegation, and cloud handoff — not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Devin CLI effectively. Devin is the 5th executor kind in the cli-* family alongside cli-codex (OpenAI), cli-claude-code (Anthropic), cli-opencode (OpenCode), and cli-cursor (Cursor).
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, architecture, or security
35: - Devin's strengths (multi-model selection, subagent delegation, cloud handoff, Adaptive routing) complement the calling AI's strengths
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks through subagents while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: - You need to offload long-running tasks to a cloud VM with browser and shell access
39: - You want cross-AI validation from a Cognition-backed model
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
44: 
45: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
46: 
47: ### Flow
48: 
49: ```
50: Calling AI (plan) --> Devin CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Devin CLI (fix)
51: ```
52: 
53: ### Implementation
54: 
55: ```bash
56: # Step 1: Devin generates the code
57: devin -p \
58:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
59:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
60: 
61: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
62: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
63: 
64: # Step 3: Devin fixes based on review
65: devin -p \
66:   "@/tmp/rate-limiter.ts Fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
67:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
68: ```
69: 
70: ### When to Use
71: 
72: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
73: - Complex algorithms where verification matters more than speed
74: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
75: 
76: ### Considerations
77: 
78: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
79: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
80: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
81: 
82: ---
83: 
84: ## 3. SUBAGENT DELEGATION FOR PARALLEL WORK
85: 
86: **Devin's unique strength: native subagent spawning for independent parallel tasks.**
87: 
88: ### Flow
89: 
90: ```
91: Calling AI (plan) --> Devin CLI (spawn subagents) --> [explore-1, explore-2, explore-3] --> Devin (summarize) --> Calling AI
92: ```
93: 
94: ### Implementation
95: 
96: ```bash
97: # Dispatch Devin to spawn multiple explore subagents for independent research
98: devin -p \
99:   "Spawn three subagent_explore subagents: one to map the API layer, one to map the database layer, and one to map the auth layer. Run them in the background. When all three complete, summarize the key files, dependencies, and any circular imports found." \
100:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto > /tmp/subagent-summary.txt 2>&1
101: 
102: # Calling AI reads the summary
103: cat /tmp/subagent-summary.txt
104: ```
105: 
106: ### When to Use
107: 
108: - Independent research tasks that can run in parallel
109: - Codebase exploration across multiple modules simultaneously
110: - Gathering context before a major implementation effort
111: 
112: ### Considerations
113: 
114: - `subagent_explore` runs on the cheap default subagent model (SWE-1.6) — cost-effective
115: - `subagent_general` inherits the parent's model — more expensive, use for code changes
116: - Background subagents cannot prompt for new permissions — pre-approve tools first
117: - Each subagent has its own context window — they do not inherit the parent's conversation history
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
122: 
123: **Run Devin tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
124: 
125: ### Implementation
126: 
127: ```bash
128: # Launch multiple Devin tasks in background
129: devin -p "Review src/api/ for security vulnerabilities. Return structured findings." \
130:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-review.txt 2>&1 &
131: PID1=$!
132: 
133: devin -p "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
134:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
135: PID2=$!
136: 
137: # Calling AI continues other work...
138: 
139: # Wait for specific task
140: wait $PID1
141: echo "Security review complete"
142: cat /tmp/security-review.txt | head -20
143: 
144: # Wait for all
145: wait $PID1 $PID2
146: echo "All Devin tasks complete"
147: ```
148: 
149: ### Monitoring
150: 
151: ```bash
152: # Check if still running
153: kill -0 $PID1 2>/dev/null && echo "Still running" || echo "Complete"
154: 
155: # Check output size (proxy for progress)
156: wc -c /tmp/security-review.txt
157: 
158: # Tail streaming output
159: tail -f /tmp/generated-tests.ts
160: ```
161: 
162: ### When to Use
163: 
164: - Independent tasks that do not depend on each other
165: - Long-running analysis while the calling AI handles quick edits
166: - Generating multiple artifacts simultaneously (tests, docs, types)
167: 
168: ### Considerations
169: 
170: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
171: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 devin -p ...` to prevent hung processes
172: - Do not background tasks with `--permission-mode accept-edits` or higher that write to the same files (race conditions)
173: - Background `--permission-mode auto` (read-only) tasks are safe to parallelize freely
174: 
175: ### False-Completion Trap When Launching from Another AI's Bash Tool
176: 
177: When an orchestrating AI uses its `Bash` tool to launch `devin -p ... &`, the shell command returns exit 0 immediately because the `&` backgrounds the process and the parent shell exits. The orchestrating AI's task system reports "completed" even though the devin process is still running.
178: 
179: **Symptom:** All 5 parallel devin sessions "complete" in under 2 seconds. Output files are empty or missing.
180: 
181: **Root cause:** The Bash tool wraps the command in a subshell. `devin -p ... &` forks the process, the subshell exits, and the task system sees exit 0.
182: 
183: ```bash
184: # BAD: Reports instant "completion" to the orchestrator
185: devin -p "..." --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt &
186: echo "PID: $!"
187: # Shell exits immediately. Orchestrator thinks task is done.
188: 
189: # GOOD: Let the Bash tool wait for devin to finish
190: devin -p "..." --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt
191: # Bash tool blocks until devin completes. Use run_in_background on the Bash call itself.
192: ```
193: 
194: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
195: 
196: When a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `devin -p ... &` inside the loop body, **devin silently consumes the loop's stdin**. The loop exits after the first 3-6 iterations with no error, dropping most dispatches.
197: 
198: **Symptom:** You dispatch a 27-finding batch; only 3-6 devin processes actually launch. No error, no warning.
199: 
200: **Root cause:** `devin -p` inherits the script's stdin by default. Each backgrounded devin process reads from the same file descriptor and races with the `read` command for lines.
201: 
202: ```bash
203: # BAD: devin inherits the loop's stdin, drains input.jsonl after iteration ~3
204: while IFS= read -r line; do
205:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
206:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
207: done < input.jsonl
208: 
209: # GOOD: redirect devin stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
210: while IFS= read -r line; do
211:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
212:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
213: done < input.jsonl
214: ```
215: 
216: **Always pair `devin -p ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.**
217: 
218: ---
219: 
220: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
221: 
222: **Devin CLI supports multiple models from multiple providers. Choose based on task type.**
223: 
224: ### Decision Matrix
225: 
226: | Task Type | Model | Flag | Rationale |
227: |-----------|-------|------|-----------|
228: | General delegation | `adaptive` | `--model adaptive` | Router auto-selects best model per task |
229: | Architecture analysis | `opus` | `--model opus` | Deep reasoning for complex analysis |
230: | Security audit | `opus` | `--model opus` | Catches subtle vulnerability patterns |
231: | Complex planning | `opus` / `adaptive` | `--model opus` | Multi-strategy evaluation |
232: | Research synthesis | `sonnet` / `adaptive` | `--model sonnet` | Good synthesis at reasonable cost |
233: | Code generation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Balanced for code output |
234: | Standard review | `sonnet` / `adaptive` | `--model sonnet` | Efficient pattern-based review |
235: | Implementation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Balanced for spec-to-code |
236: | Test generation | `gpt` / `adaptive` | `--model gpt` | Solid test structure |
237: | Documentation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Efficient structured generation |
238: | Quick edits | `swe-1-6-fast` | `--model swe-1-6-fast` | Minimize latency and cost |
239: | Cost-sensitive | `swe` / `adaptive` | `--model swe` | Reasonable intelligence at low cost |
240: 
241: ### Implementation
242: 
243: ```bash
244: # Deep analysis with Opus
245: devin -p "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
246:   --model opus --permission-mode auto
247: 
248: # Code-focused tasks with Adaptive
249: devin -p "Write tests for utils.ts" \
250:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
251: 
252: # Quick edits with SWE Fast
253: devin -p "Fix the typo in the error message at line 42" \
254:   --model swe-1-6-fast --permission-mode accept-edits
255: 
256: # Mixed workflow: analyze with Opus, implement with Adaptive
257: devin -p "Identify all security vulnerabilities in src/auth/" \
258:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-findings.txt
259: 
260: devin -p "Fix these security issues: $(cat /tmp/security-findings.txt)" \
261:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
262: ```
263: 
264: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
265: 
266: - Omitting `--model` relies on the CLI default from `~/.config/devin/config.json`, which may differ across machines
267: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
268: - The model can also be set in the config file as a project-level default
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 6. PERMISSION MODE STRATEGY
273: 
274: **Choose the least-permissive mode that allows the task to succeed.**
275: 
276: ### Decision Flow
277: 
278: ```
279: Task type?
280:   |
281:   +-- Analysis / review / exploration --> auto
282:   |
283:   +-- Code generation / refactoring --> accept-edits
284:   |
285:   +-- Trusted workflow with judgment calls --> smart
286:   |
287:   +-- System operations / full auto --> dangerous (ASK USER FIRST)
288:   |
289:   +-- Unattended execution with OS limits --> --sandbox (autonomous)
290: ```
291: 
292: ### Implementation by Task Type
293: 
294: ```bash
295: # Analysis: auto (read-only auto-approve)
296: devin -p "Identify all N+1 query patterns in src/" \
297:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive
298: 
299: # Code generation: accept-edits
300: devin -p "Add retry logic to all API calls in src/api/" \
301:   --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive
302: 
303: # Unattended execution: sandbox
304: devin --sandbox -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" \
305:   --model adaptive
306: 
307: # Preview before committing: auto first, accept-edits after review
308: devin -p "List all files that would be changed by the auth refactor" \
309:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive > /tmp/files-to-change.txt
310: # Review /tmp/files-to-change.txt, then proceed:
311: devin -p "Apply the auth refactor to the files listed in /tmp/files-to-change.txt" \
312:   --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive
313: ```
314: 
315: ### Mode Combinations to Avoid
316: 
317: | Combination | Risk | Better Approach |
318: |-------------|------|-----------------|
319: | `dangerous` + unattended | Unrestricted, unreviewed changes | Use `accept-edits` or `--sandbox` instead |
320: | `accept-edits` + blind background | Parallel writes to same files | Use `auto` for parallel background tasks |
321: | `accept-edits` for pure analysis | Unnecessary write permissions | Use `auto`; it is sufficient for analysis |
322: 
323: ---
324: 
325: ## 7. CONTEXT ENRICHMENT
326: 
327: **Provide Devin with rich context for better results.**
328: 
329: ### File References
330: 
331: ```bash
332: # In the REPL, type @ to open file autocomplete
333: # @src/database.ts refactor to use the repository pattern
334: 
335: # Non-interactive with file content piped in
336: cat src/auth.ts | devin -p "Add input validation to all functions in this file" \
337:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
338: ```
339: 
340: ### Explicit Context Injection
341: 
342: ```bash
343: # Inject the calling AI's analysis as context
344: CALLING_AI_ANALYSIS="The bug is in the token refresh logic. The refresh token
345: is not being rotated on use, allowing token replay attacks."
346: 
347: devin -p \
348:   "Fix this security issue in the auth token handler. Context from prior analysis: $CALLING_AI_ANALYSIS" \
349:   --model opus --permission-mode accept-edits
350: ```
351: 
352: ### Web Research via Fetch
353: 
354: ```bash
355: # Devin can fetch URLs during execution for current information
356: devin -p "Fetch the latest Express.js 5.x migration guide and summarize the breaking changes. Implement the recommended patterns in src/app.ts." \
357:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
358: ```
359: 
360: ---
361: 
362: ## 8. VALIDATION PIPELINE
363: 
364: **Multi-stage validation of Devin-generated output.**
365: 
366: ### Implementation
367: 
368: ```bash
369: # Stage 1: Generate
370: devin -p "Create a webhook handler for Stripe events" \
371:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook.ts
372: 
373: # Stage 2: Syntax check
374: npx tsc --noEmit /tmp/webhook.ts 2>/tmp/syntax-errors.txt
375: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
376:   devin -p \
377:     "Fix these TypeScript errors in the webhook handler: $(cat /tmp/syntax-errors.txt)" \
378:     --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts
379:   cp /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts /tmp/webhook.ts
380: fi
381: 
382: # Stage 3: Security scan
383: devin -p \
384:   "Audit this webhook handler for security issues. Focus on: input validation, injection attacks, authentication bypasses. Return structured findings." \
385:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-scan.txt
386: 
387: # Stage 4: Functional check (calling AI reviews the result)
388: # Read /tmp/webhook.ts and /tmp/security-scan.txt within the calling AI
389: 
390: # Stage 5: Style alignment
391: devin -p \
392:   "Reformat the webhook handler to match project conventions. Functional style, JSDoc on exports." \
393:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook-final.ts
394: ```
395: 
396: ### Pipeline Stages (Recommended Order)
397: 
398: | Stage | Purpose | Tool |
399: |-------|---------|------|
400: | 1. Generate | Create initial artifact | Devin (`adaptive`, `accept-edits`) |
401: | 2. Syntax | Verify it compiles/parses | Language toolchain (tsc, eslint, etc.) |
402: | 3. Security | Check for vulnerabilities | Devin (`opus`, `auto`) |
403: | 4. Functional | Verify correctness | Calling AI review or tests |
404: | 5. Style | Match project conventions | Devin (`adaptive`, `accept-edits`) |
405: 
406: ### When to Use
407: 
408: - Any generated code that will be committed to the repository
409: - Security-sensitive code (auth, payments, data handling)
410: - Code that lacks test coverage
411: 
412: ---
413: 
414: ## 9. CROSS-VALIDATION WITH OTHER CLI EXECUTORS
415: 
416: **Use multiple AI executors to validate each other's work.**
417: 
418: ### Calling AI Generates, Devin Reviews
419: 
420: ```bash
421: # Calling AI generates code (within the session)
422: # Then Devin reviews it:
423: devin -p \
424:   "Review the newly-generated module for: correctness, edge cases, performance issues, and adherence to SOLID principles. Be critical. Return structured findings." \
425:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/devin-review.txt
426: ```
427: 
428: ### Devin Generates, Calling AI Reviews
429: 
430: ```bash
431: # Devin generates
432: devin -p "Create a caching layer with TTL support and LRU eviction" \
433:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/cache.ts
434: 
435: # Calling AI reviews within the session (read /tmp/cache.ts and analyze)
436: ```
437: 
438: ### Multi-Executor Consensus Check
439: 
440: ```bash
441: # Devin generates one approach
442: devin -p "Design a caching strategy for this API. Consider Redis, in-memory, and CDN approaches." \
443:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/devin-plan.txt
444: 
445: # Codex generates another approach (via cli-codex)
446: codex exec "Design a caching strategy for this API. Consider Redis, in-memory, and CDN approaches." \
447:   --model gpt-5.5 --sandbox read-only > /tmp/codex-plan.txt
448: 
449: # Calling AI compares both approaches and synthesizes
450: ```
451: 
452: ### Strength Comparison for Task Routing
453: 
454: | Strength Area | Calling AI | Devin CLI |
455: |---------------|-------------|-----------|
456: | Codebase context | Deep (built-in tools, spec-folder continuity docs) | Good (with @ file references and subagents) |
457: | Multi-model access | Single model | Multiple (Opus, Sonnet, GPT, SWE, Codex, Gemini, etc.) |
458: | Multi-file refactoring | Strong | Strong (especially with Opus) |
459: | Architecture reasoning | Strong | Strong (Opus reasoning) |
460: | Subagent delegation | Not native | Native (`run_subagent`) |
461: | Cloud execution | Not built-in | `/handoff` to cloud VM |
462: | Session continuity | Built-in (conversation context) | Via `-c` / `-r` / `/resume` / `/fork` |
463: | Spec-folder continuity | Native | Not available |
464: | Cost optimization | Single model | Adaptive router + SWE-1.6 for cheap tasks |
465: 
466: ### Cross-Validation Strategies
467: 
468: | Strategy | Flow | Best For |
469: |----------|------|----------|
470: | **Adversarial review** | A generates, B critiques | Security-critical code |
471: | **Consensus check** | Both solve independently, compare | Architectural decisions |
472: | **Specialist routing** | Route by strength (table above) | Efficiency optimization |
473: | **Red team** | A writes, B tries to break | Auth, payments, data access |
474: | **Multi-model consensus** | Devin runs multiple models internally | Tasks where model diversity helps |
475: 
476: ---
477: 
478: ## 10. SESSION CONTINUITY
479: 
480: **Maintain context across multiple Devin invocations for complex, multi-turn tasks.**
481: 
482: ### Session Operations
483: 
484: ```bash
485: # Continue the most recent session
486: devin -c
487: 
488: # Resume a specific session by ID
489: devin -r brisk-otter
490: 
491: # Non-interactive continuation
492: devin -c -p "Continue implementing the rate limiter from where we left off" \
493:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
494: 
495: # List sessions
496: devin list --format json
497: ```
498: 
499: ### Multi-Turn Scripted Workflow
500: 
501: ```bash
502: # Turn 1: Analysis - capture session ID from output
503: devin -p "Analyze src/auth/ architecture. List 5 improvements." \
504:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/analysis.txt
505: # Note the session ID from the output or session list
506: 
507: # Turn 2: Implement first improvement (continue same session)
508: devin -c -p "Implement improvement #1 from your analysis" \
509:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
510: 
511: # Fork before trying a risky approach (inside REPL)
512: # /fork
513: ```
514: 
515: ### When to Use Each Operation
516: 
517: | Operation | When to Use |
518: |-----------|-------------|
519: | `-c` / continue | Continue the most recent session with existing context |
520: | `-r` / resume | Resume a specific session by ID |
521: | `/fork` | Try a different approach without losing the original session state |
522: | New session | Fresh context; prior session is not relevant |
523: | `-p` (stateless) | One-shot tasks; simpler to re-provide context than manage sessions |
524: 
525: ### Considerations
526: 
527: - For cross-AI orchestration, it is often simpler to re-provide context via file references than to manage session IDs across multiple `devin -p` calls.
528: - Use sessions when the task genuinely builds on prior Devin reasoning that would be costly to re-establish.
529: - Fork before any operation that could leave the session in a broken state.
530: 
531: ---
532: 
533: ## 11. ANTI-PATTERNS
534: 
535: **What NOT to do when orchestrating Devin CLI from the calling AI.**
536: 
537: ### 1. Using dangerous Mode Without Approval
538: 
539: ```bash
540: # BAD: Dangerous mode on destructive operations without human checkpoint
541: devin -p "Clean up the codebase" --permission-mode dangerous
542: 
543: # GOOD: Review plan first, then execute with appropriate mode
544: devin -p "List files that could be cleaned up. Do not delete anything." \
545:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive
546: # Review the list, then selectively execute
547: ```
548: 
549: ### 2. Trusting Output Blindly
550: 
551: ```bash
552: # BAD: Direct pipe to production
553: devin -p "Generate migration SQL" --model adaptive --permission-mode auto \
554:   | psql production_db
555: 
556: # GOOD: Generate, review, test, then apply
557: devin -p "Generate migration SQL" --model adaptive --permission-mode auto \
558:   > /tmp/migration.sql
559: # Review /tmp/migration.sql
560: # Test on staging: psql staging_db -f /tmp/migration.sql
561: # Then apply to production
562: ```
563: 
564: ### 3. Over-Specifying in a Single Prompt
565: 
566: ```bash
567: # BAD: Everything at once
568: devin -p "Create a complete REST API with auth, CRUD, rate limiting, caching, logging, monitoring, tests, and deployment config" \
569:   --model adaptive
570: 
571: # GOOD: Incremental
572: devin -p "Create type definitions for a blog API: User, Post, Comment" \
573:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
574: # Then build on top incrementally
575: ```
576: 
577: ### 4. Background Tasks Writing the Same Files
578: 
579: ```bash
580: # BAD: Parallel writes to overlapping files
581: devin -p "Fix auth" --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive &
582: devin -p "Fix auth tests" --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive &
583: # Race condition: both modify src/auth/ simultaneously
584: 
585: # GOOD: Background only for independent, read-only analysis
586: devin -p "Review src/auth/" --permission-mode auto --model opus > /tmp/auth-review.txt &
587: devin -p "Review src/payments/" --permission-mode auto --model opus > /tmp/pay-review.txt &
588: wait
589: ```
590: 
591: ### 5. Backgrounding devin Inside Shell Scripts Called by Another AI
592: 
593: ```bash
594: # BAD: & inside the shell command - orchestrator sees instant exit 0
595: devin -p "Deep review all phases" --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt 2>&1 &
596: echo "PID: $!"
597: # The Bash tool reports "completed" in <2 seconds. Devin is still running.
598: 
599: # GOOD: No & - use the orchestrator's own background mechanism instead
600: devin -p "Deep review all phases" --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt 2>&1
601: # The orchestrator waits for the actual devin process to finish.
602: ```
603: 
604: ### 6. Forgetting Context in Stateless -p Calls
605: 
606: ```bash
607: # BAD: Follow-up without re-providing context
608: devin -p "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model adaptive  # Turn 1
609: devin -p "Now fix the issue you found" --model adaptive  # Turn 2: Devin has no memory of Turn 1
610: 
611: # GOOD: Re-provide context or use session continue
612: devin -p "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model adaptive > /tmp/analysis.txt
613: devin -p "Fix the issues identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
614:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
615: ```
616: 
617: ### 7. Using subagent_general for Read-Only Research
618: 
619: ```bash
620: # BAD: general subagent runs on parent's (possibly expensive) model for research
621: devin -p "Use a subagent_general subagent to research the auth module" \
622:   --model opus --permission-mode auto
623: 
624: # GOOD: explore subagent runs on cheap SWE-1.6 for read-only research
625: devin -p "Use a subagent_explore subagent to research the auth module" \
626:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto
627: ```

15: 
16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Devin CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Devin CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Devin CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives and leveraging Devin's multi-model surface, subagent delegation, and cloud handoff — not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Devin CLI effectively. Devin is the 5th executor kind in the cli-* family alongside cli-codex (OpenAI), cli-claude-code (Anthropic), cli-opencode (OpenCode), and cli-cursor (Cursor).
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, architecture, or security
35: - Devin's strengths (multi-model selection, subagent delegation, cloud handoff, Adaptive routing) complement the calling AI's strengths
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks through subagents while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: - You need to offload long-running tasks to a cloud VM with browser and shell access
39: - You want cross-AI validation from a Cognition-backed model
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
44: 
45: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
46: 
47: ### Flow
48: 
49: ```
50: Calling AI (plan) --> Devin CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Devin CLI (fix)
51: ```
52: 
53: ### Implementation
54: 
55: ```bash
56: # Step 1: Devin generates the code
57: devin -p \
58:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
59:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
60: 
61: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
62: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
63: 
64: # Step 3: Devin fixes based on review
65: devin -p \
66:   "@/tmp/rate-limiter.ts Fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
67:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
68: ```
69: 
70: ### When to Use
71: 
72: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
73: - Complex algorithms where verification matters more than speed
74: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
75: 
76: ### Considerations
77: 
78: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
79: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
80: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
81: 
82: ---
83: 
84: ## 3. SUBAGENT DELEGATION FOR PARALLEL WORK
85: 
86: **Devin's unique strength: native subagent spawning for independent parallel tasks.**
87: 
88: ### Flow
89: 
90: ```
91: Calling AI (plan) --> Devin CLI (spawn subagents) --> [explore-1, explore-2, explore-3] --> Devin (summarize) --> Calling AI
92: ```
93: 
94: ### Implementation
95: 
96: ```bash
97: # Dispatch Devin to spawn multiple explore subagents for independent research
98: devin -p \
99:   "Spawn three subagent_explore subagents: one to map the API layer, one to map the database layer, and one to map the auth layer. Run them in the background. When all three complete, summarize the key files, dependencies, and any circular imports found." \
100:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto > /tmp/subagent-summary.txt 2>&1
101: 
102: # Calling AI reads the summary
103: cat /tmp/subagent-summary.txt
104: ```
105: 
106: ### When to Use
107: 
108: - Independent research tasks that can run in parallel
109: - Codebase exploration across multiple modules simultaneously
110: - Gathering context before a major implementation effort
111: 
112: ### Considerations
113: 
114: - `subagent_explore` runs on the cheap default subagent model (SWE-1.6) — cost-effective
115: - `subagent_general` inherits the parent's model — more expensive, use for code changes
116: - Background subagents cannot prompt for new permissions — pre-approve tools first
117: - Each subagent has its own context window — they do not inherit the parent's conversation history
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
122: 
123: **Run Devin tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
124: 
125: ### Implementation
126: 
127: ```bash
128: # Launch multiple Devin tasks in background
129: devin -p "Review src/api/ for security vulnerabilities. Return structured findings." \
130:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-review.txt 2>&1 &
131: PID1=$!
132: 
133: devin -p "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
134:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
135: PID2=$!
136: 
137: # Calling AI continues other work...
138: 
139: # Wait for specific task
140: wait $PID1
141: echo "Security review complete"
142: cat /tmp/security-review.txt | head -20
143: 
144: # Wait for all
145: wait $PID1 $PID2
146: echo "All Devin tasks complete"
147: ```
148: 
149: ### Monitoring
150: 
151: ```bash
152: # Check if still running
153: kill -0 $PID1 2>/dev/null && echo "Still running" || echo "Complete"
154: 
155: # Check output size (proxy for progress)
156: wc -c /tmp/security-review.txt
157: 
158: # Tail streaming output
159: tail -f /tmp/generated-tests.ts
160: ```
161: 
162: ### When to Use
163: 
164: - Independent tasks that do not depend on each other
165: - Long-running analysis while the calling AI handles quick edits
166: - Generating multiple artifacts simultaneously (tests, docs, types)
167: 
168: ### Considerations
169: 
170: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
171: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 devin -p ...` to prevent hung processes
172: - Do not background tasks with `--permission-mode accept-edits` or higher that write to the same files (race conditions)
173: - Background `--permission-mode auto` (read-only) tasks are safe to parallelize freely
174: 
175: ### False-Completion Trap When Launching from Another AI's Bash Tool
176: 
177: When an orchestrating AI uses its `Bash` tool to launch `devin -p ... &`, the shell command returns exit 0 immediately because the `&` backgrounds the process and the parent shell exits. The orchestrating AI's task system reports "completed" even though the devin process is still running.
178: 
179: **Symptom:** All 5 parallel devin sessions "complete" in under 2 seconds. Output files are empty or missing.
180: 
181: **Root cause:** The Bash tool wraps the command in a subshell. `devin -p ... &` forks the process, the subshell exits, and the task system sees exit 0.
182: 
183: ```bash
184: # BAD: Reports instant "completion" to the orchestrator
185: devin -p "..." --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt &
186: echo "PID: $!"
187: # Shell exits immediately. Orchestrator thinks task is done.
188: 
189: # GOOD: Let the Bash tool wait for devin to finish
190: devin -p "..." --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt
191: # Bash tool blocks until devin completes. Use run_in_background on the Bash call itself.
192: ```
193: 
194: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
195: 
196: When a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `devin -p ... &` inside the loop body, **devin silently consumes the loop's stdin**. The loop exits after the first 3-6 iterations with no error, dropping most dispatches.
197: 
198: **Symptom:** You dispatch a 27-finding batch; only 3-6 devin processes actually launch. No error, no warning.
199: 
200: **Root cause:** `devin -p` inherits the script's stdin by default. Each backgrounded devin process reads from the same file descriptor and races with the `read` command for lines.
201: 
202: ```bash
203: # BAD: devin inherits the loop's stdin, drains input.jsonl after iteration ~3
204: while IFS= read -r line; do
205:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
206:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
207: done < input.jsonl
208: 
209: # GOOD: redirect devin stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
210: while IFS= read -r line; do
211:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
212:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
213: done < input.jsonl
214: ```
215: 
216: **Always pair `devin -p ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.**
217: 
218: ---
219: 
220: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
221: 
222: **Devin CLI supports multiple models from multiple providers. Choose based on task type.**
223: 
224: ### Decision Matrix
225: 
226: | Task Type | Model | Flag | Rationale |
227: |-----------|-------|------|-----------|
228: | General delegation | `adaptive` | `--model adaptive` | Router auto-selects best model per task |
229: | Architecture analysis | `opus` | `--model opus` | Deep reasoning for complex analysis |
230: | Security audit | `opus` | `--model opus` | Catches subtle vulnerability patterns |
231: | Complex planning | `opus` / `adaptive` | `--model opus` | Multi-strategy evaluation |
232: | Research synthesis | `sonnet` / `adaptive` | `--model sonnet` | Good synthesis at reasonable cost |
233: | Code generation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Balanced for code output |
234: | Standard review | `sonnet` / `adaptive` | `--model sonnet` | Efficient pattern-based review |
235: | Implementation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Balanced for spec-to-code |
236: | Test generation | `gpt` / `adaptive` | `--model gpt` | Solid test structure |
237: | Documentation | `adaptive` / `sonnet` | `--model adaptive` | Efficient structured generation |
238: | Quick edits | `swe-1-6-fast` | `--model swe-1-6-fast` | Minimize latency and cost |
239: | Cost-sensitive | `swe` / `adaptive` | `--model swe` | Reasonable intelligence at low cost |
240: 
241: ### Implementation
242: 
243: ```bash
244: # Deep analysis with Opus
245: devin -p "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
246:   --model opus --permission-mode auto
247: 
248: # Code-focused tasks with Adaptive
249: devin -p "Write tests for utils.ts" \
250:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
251: 
252: # Quick edits with SWE Fast
253: devin -p "Fix the typo in the error message at line 42" \
254:   --model swe-1-6-fast --permission-mode accept-edits
255: 
256: # Mixed workflow: analyze with Opus, implement with Adaptive
257: devin -p "Identify all security vulnerabilities in src/auth/" \
258:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-findings.txt
259: 
260: devin -p "Fix these security issues: $(cat /tmp/security-findings.txt)" \
261:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
262: ```
263: 
264: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
265: 
266: - Omitting `--model` relies on the CLI default from `~/.config/devin/config.json`, which may differ across machines
267: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
268: - The model can also be set in the config file as a project-level default
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 6. PERMISSION MODE STRATEGY
273: 
274: **Choose the least-permissive mode that allows the task to succeed.**
275: 
276: ### Decision Flow
277: 
278: ```
279: Task type?
280:   |
281:   +-- Analysis / review / exploration --> auto
282:   |
283:   +-- Code generation / refactoring --> accept-edits
284:   |
285:   +-- Trusted workflow with judgment calls --> smart
286:   |
287:   +-- System operations / full auto --> dangerous (ASK USER FIRST)
288:   |
289:   +-- Unattended execution with OS limits --> --sandbox (autonomous)
290: ```
291: 
292: ### Implementation by Task Type
293: 
294: ```bash
295: # Analysis: auto (read-only auto-approve)
296: devin -p "Identify all N+1 query patterns in src/" \
297:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive
298: 
299: # Code generation: accept-edits
300: devin -p "Add retry logic to all API calls in src/api/" \
301:   --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive
302: 
303: # Unattended execution: sandbox
304: devin --sandbox -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" \
305:   --model adaptive
306: 
307: # Preview before committing: auto first, accept-edits after review
308: devin -p "List all files that would be changed by the auth refactor" \
309:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive > /tmp/files-to-change.txt
310: # Review /tmp/files-to-change.txt, then proceed:
311: devin -p "Apply the auth refactor to the files listed in /tmp/files-to-change.txt" \
312:   --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive
313: ```
314: 
315: ### Mode Combinations to Avoid
316: 
317: | Combination | Risk | Better Approach |
318: |-------------|------|-----------------|
319: | `dangerous` + unattended | Unrestricted, unreviewed changes | Use `accept-edits` or `--sandbox` instead |
320: | `accept-edits` + blind background | Parallel writes to same files | Use `auto` for parallel background tasks |
321: | `accept-edits` for pure analysis | Unnecessary write permissions | Use `auto`; it is sufficient for analysis |
322: 
323: ---
324: 
325: ## 7. CONTEXT ENRICHMENT
326: 
327: **Provide Devin with rich context for better results.**
328: 
329: ### File References
330: 
331: ```bash
332: # In the REPL, type @ to open file autocomplete
333: # @src/database.ts refactor to use the repository pattern
334: 
335: # Non-interactive with file content piped in
336: cat src/auth.ts | devin -p "Add input validation to all functions in this file" \
337:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
338: ```
339: 
340: ### Explicit Context Injection
341: 
342: ```bash
343: # Inject the calling AI's analysis as context
344: CALLING_AI_ANALYSIS="The bug is in the token refresh logic. The refresh token
345: is not being rotated on use, allowing token replay attacks."
346: 
347: devin -p \
348:   "Fix this security issue in the auth token handler. Context from prior analysis: $CALLING_AI_ANALYSIS" \
349:   --model opus --permission-mode accept-edits
350: ```
351: 
352: ### Web Research via Fetch
353: 
354: ```bash
355: # Devin can fetch URLs during execution for current information
356: devin -p "Fetch the latest Express.js 5.x migration guide and summarize the breaking changes. Implement the recommended patterns in src/app.ts." \
357:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
358: ```
359: 
360: ---
361: 
362: ## 8. VALIDATION PIPELINE
363: 
364: **Multi-stage validation of Devin-generated output.**
365: 
366: ### Implementation
367: 
368: ```bash
369: # Stage 1: Generate
370: devin -p "Create a webhook handler for Stripe events" \
371:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook.ts
372: 
373: # Stage 2: Syntax check
374: npx tsc --noEmit /tmp/webhook.ts 2>/tmp/syntax-errors.txt
375: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
376:   devin -p \
377:     "Fix these TypeScript errors in the webhook handler: $(cat /tmp/syntax-errors.txt)" \
378:     --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts
379:   cp /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts /tmp/webhook.ts
380: fi
381: 
382: # Stage 3: Security scan
383: devin -p \
384:   "Audit this webhook handler for security issues. Focus on: input validation, injection attacks, authentication bypasses. Return structured findings." \
385:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/security-scan.txt
386: 
387: # Stage 4: Functional check (calling AI reviews the result)
388: # Read /tmp/webhook.ts and /tmp/security-scan.txt within the calling AI
389: 
390: # Stage 5: Style alignment
391: devin -p \
392:   "Reformat the webhook handler to match project conventions. Functional style, JSDoc on exports." \
393:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/webhook-final.ts
394: ```
395: 
396: ### Pipeline Stages (Recommended Order)
397: 
398: | Stage | Purpose | Tool |
399: |-------|---------|------|
400: | 1. Generate | Create initial artifact | Devin (`adaptive`, `accept-edits`) |
401: | 2. Syntax | Verify it compiles/parses | Language toolchain (tsc, eslint, etc.) |
402: | 3. Security | Check for vulnerabilities | Devin (`opus`, `auto`) |
403: | 4. Functional | Verify correctness | Calling AI review or tests |
404: | 5. Style | Match project conventions | Devin (`adaptive`, `accept-edits`) |
405: 
406: ### When to Use
407: 
408: - Any generated code that will be committed to the repository
409: - Security-sensitive code (auth, payments, data handling)
410: - Code that lacks test coverage
411: 
412: ---
413: 
414: ## 9. CROSS-VALIDATION WITH OTHER CLI EXECUTORS
415: 
416: **Use multiple AI executors to validate each other's work.**
417: 
418: ### Calling AI Generates, Devin Reviews
419: 
420: ```bash
421: # Calling AI generates code (within the session)
422: # Then Devin reviews it:
423: devin -p \
424:   "Review the newly-generated module for: correctness, edge cases, performance issues, and adherence to SOLID principles. Be critical. Return structured findings." \
425:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/devin-review.txt
426: ```
427: 
428: ### Devin Generates, Calling AI Reviews
429: 
430: ```bash
431: # Devin generates
432: devin -p "Create a caching layer with TTL support and LRU eviction" \
433:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/cache.ts
434: 
435: # Calling AI reviews within the session (read /tmp/cache.ts and analyze)
436: ```
437: 
438: ### Multi-Executor Consensus Check
439: 
440: ```bash
441: # Devin generates one approach
442: devin -p "Design a caching strategy for this API. Consider Redis, in-memory, and CDN approaches." \
443:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/devin-plan.txt
444: 
445: # Codex generates another approach (via cli-codex)
446: codex exec "Design a caching strategy for this API. Consider Redis, in-memory, and CDN approaches." \
447:   --model gpt-5.5 --sandbox read-only > /tmp/codex-plan.txt
448: 
449: # Calling AI compares both approaches and synthesizes
450: ```
451: 
452: ### Strength Comparison for Task Routing
453: 
454: | Strength Area | Calling AI | Devin CLI |
455: |---------------|-------------|-----------|
456: | Codebase context | Deep (built-in tools, spec-folder continuity docs) | Good (with @ file references and subagents) |
457: | Multi-model access | Single model | Multiple (Opus, Sonnet, GPT, SWE, Codex, Gemini, etc.) |
458: | Multi-file refactoring | Strong | Strong (especially with Opus) |
459: | Architecture reasoning | Strong | Strong (Opus reasoning) |
460: | Subagent delegation | Not native | Native (`run_subagent`) |
461: | Cloud execution | Not built-in | `/handoff` to cloud VM |
462: | Session continuity | Built-in (conversation context) | Via `-c` / `-r` / `/resume` / `/fork` |
463: | Spec-folder continuity | Native | Not available |
464: | Cost optimization | Single model | Adaptive router + SWE-1.6 for cheap tasks |
465: 
466: ### Cross-Validation Strategies
467: 
468: | Strategy | Flow | Best For |
469: |----------|------|----------|
470: | **Adversarial review** | A generates, B critiques | Security-critical code |
471: | **Consensus check** | Both solve independently, compare | Architectural decisions |
472: | **Specialist routing** | Route by strength (table above) | Efficiency optimization |
473: | **Red team** | A writes, B tries to break | Auth, payments, data access |
474: | **Multi-model consensus** | Devin runs multiple models internally | Tasks where model diversity helps |
475: 
476: ---
477: 
478: ## 10. SESSION CONTINUITY
479: 
480: **Maintain context across multiple Devin invocations for complex, multi-turn tasks.**
481: 
482: ### Session Operations
483: 
484: ```bash
485: # Continue the most recent session
486: devin -c
487: 
488: # Resume a specific session by ID
489: devin -r brisk-otter
490: 
491: # Non-interactive continuation
492: devin -c -p "Continue implementing the rate limiter from where we left off" \
493:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
494: 
495: # List sessions
496: devin list --format json
497: ```
498: 
499: ### Multi-Turn Scripted Workflow
500: 
501: ```bash
502: # Turn 1: Analysis - capture session ID from output
503: devin -p "Analyze src/auth/ architecture. List 5 improvements." \
504:   --model opus --permission-mode auto > /tmp/analysis.txt
505: # Note the session ID from the output or session list
506: 
507: # Turn 2: Implement first improvement (continue same session)
508: devin -c -p "Implement improvement #1 from your analysis" \
509:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
510: 
511: # Fork before trying a risky approach (inside REPL)
512: # /fork
513: ```
514: 
515: ### When to Use Each Operation
516: 
517: | Operation | When to Use |
518: |-----------|-------------|
519: | `-c` / continue | Continue the most recent session with existing context |
520: | `-r` / resume | Resume a specific session by ID |
521: | `/fork` | Try a different approach without losing the original session state |
522: | New session | Fresh context; prior session is not relevant |
523: | `-p` (stateless) | One-shot tasks; simpler to re-provide context than manage sessions |
524: 
525: ### Considerations
526: 
527: - For cross-AI orchestration, it is often simpler to re-provide context via file references than to manage session IDs across multiple `devin -p` calls.
528: - Use sessions when the task genuinely builds on prior Devin reasoning that would be costly to re-establish.
529: - Fork before any operation that could leave the session in a broken state.
530: 
531: ---
532: 
533: ## 11. ANTI-PATTERNS
534: 
535: **What NOT to do when orchestrating Devin CLI from the calling AI.**
536: 
537: ### 1. Using dangerous Mode Without Approval
538: 
539: ```bash
540: # BAD: Dangerous mode on destructive operations without human checkpoint
541: devin -p "Clean up the codebase" --permission-mode dangerous
542: 
543: # GOOD: Review plan first, then execute with appropriate mode
544: devin -p "List files that could be cleaned up. Do not delete anything." \
545:   --permission-mode auto --model adaptive
546: # Review the list, then selectively execute
547: ```
548: 
549: ### 2. Trusting Output Blindly
550: 
551: ```bash
552: # BAD: Direct pipe to production
553: devin -p "Generate migration SQL" --model adaptive --permission-mode auto \
554:   | psql production_db
555: 
556: # GOOD: Generate, review, test, then apply
557: devin -p "Generate migration SQL" --model adaptive --permission-mode auto \
558:   > /tmp/migration.sql
559: # Review /tmp/migration.sql
560: # Test on staging: psql staging_db -f /tmp/migration.sql
561: # Then apply to production
562: ```
563: 
564: ### 3. Over-Specifying in a Single Prompt
565: 
566: ```bash
567: # BAD: Everything at once
568: devin -p "Create a complete REST API with auth, CRUD, rate limiting, caching, logging, monitoring, tests, and deployment config" \
569:   --model adaptive
570: 
571: # GOOD: Incremental
572: devin -p "Create type definitions for a blog API: User, Post, Comment" \
573:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
574: # Then build on top incrementally
575: ```
576: 
577: ### 4. Background Tasks Writing the Same Files
578: 
579: ```bash
580: # BAD: Parallel writes to overlapping files
581: devin -p "Fix auth" --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive &
582: devin -p "Fix auth tests" --permission-mode accept-edits --model adaptive &
583: # Race condition: both modify src/auth/ simultaneously
584: 
585: # GOOD: Background only for independent, read-only analysis
586: devin -p "Review src/auth/" --permission-mode auto --model opus > /tmp/auth-review.txt &
587: devin -p "Review src/payments/" --permission-mode auto --model opus > /tmp/pay-review.txt &
588: wait
589: ```

591: ### 5. Backgrounding devin Inside Shell Scripts Called by Another AI
592: 
593: ```bash
594: # BAD: & inside the shell command - orchestrator sees instant exit 0
595: devin -p "Deep review all phases" --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt 2>&1 &
596: echo "PID: $!"
597: # The Bash tool reports "completed" in <2 seconds. Devin is still running.
598: 
599: # GOOD: No & - use the orchestrator's own background mechanism instead
600: devin -p "Deep review all phases" --permission-mode accept-edits > /tmp/result.txt 2>&1
601: # The orchestrator waits for the actual devin process to finish.
602: ```

605: 
606: ```bash
607: # BAD: Follow-up without re-providing context
608: devin -p "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model adaptive  # Turn 1
609: devin -p "Now fix the issue you found" --model adaptive  # Turn 2: Devin has no memory of Turn 1
610: 
611: # GOOD: Re-provide context or use session continue
612: devin -p "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model adaptive > /tmp/analysis.txt
613: devin -p "Fix the issues identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
614:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
615: ```
616: 
617: ### 7. Using subagent_general for Read-Only Research
618: 
619: ```bash
620: # BAD: general subagent runs on parent's (possibly expensive) model for research
621: devin -p "Use a subagent_general subagent to research the auth module" \
622:   --model opus --permission-mode auto
623: 
624: # GOOD: explore subagent runs on cheap SWE-1.6 for read-only research
625: devin -p "Use a subagent_explore subagent to research the auth module" \
626:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto
627: ```

17: # Devin CLI Built-in Tools Reference
18: 
19: Reference for all Devin CLI capabilities, highlighting unique features and the 4-tier permission model.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: ### Core Principle
26: 
27: Delegate to Devin CLI for capabilities the calling AI lacks natively — especially `run_subagent` for parallel subagent delegation, `/handoff` for cloud session transfer, multi-model selection, and the OS-level sandbox for autonomous execution.

32: 
33: ### When to Use
34: 
35: - Choosing whether to delegate a task to Devin CLI or handle it in the calling AI

37: - Mapping calling AI capabilities to Devin CLI equivalents

39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 2. UNIQUE CAPABILITIES
43: 
44: These capabilities are exclusive to Devin CLI or provide significantly different workflows.
45: 
46: ### run_subagent Tool
47: 
48: **Native subagent spawning for parallel work.** Devin's `run_subagent` tool lets the parent agent spawn independent workers that share tools and codebase context but operate in their own conversation chain.
49: 
50: **Capabilities:**
51: - Two built-in profiles: `subagent_explore` (read-only, cheap SWE-1.6) and `subagent_general` (full access, parent's model)
52: - Custom profiles via `.devin/agents/[name]/AGENT.md` with model overrides and tool restrictions
53: - Foreground (parent pauses) or background (parallel) execution
54: - Background subagents auto-deny unapproved tools; foreground subagents prompt for approval
55: - Subagents can be resumed in the foreground if they fail due to denied tools
56: 
57: **Usage:**
58: 
59: ```bash
60: # Request an explore subagent for read-only research
61: devin -p "Research the auth module using a subagent_explore subagent" \
62:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto
63: 
64: # Request a general subagent for code changes
65: devin -p "Fix the failing tests using a subagent_general subagent" \
66:   --model adaptive --permission-mode accept-edits
67: ```
68: 
69: **Best For:**
70: - Parallel research across multiple modules
71: - Cost-effective exploration (explore subagent runs on SWE-1.6)
72: - Specialized workers via custom AGENT.md profiles
73: - Isolating subtask context from the parent conversation
74: 
75: **Compared to other CLI executors:** Most CLI executors lack native subagent spawning. Devin's `run_subagent` is a first-class tool that the agent calls automatically when a task benefits from independent work.
76: 
77: Full subagent details: [agent-delegation.md](./agent-delegation.md)
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ### /handoff Command
82: 
83: **Cloud session transfer.** The `/handoff` command transfers the current session to a cloud Devin session with its own VM, shell, browser, and full repo access.
84: 
85: **Capabilities:**
86: - Packages conversation context and current git branch
87: - Cloud session clones the right repo and checks out the branch
88: - Uncommitted changes (work-in-progress diff) carry over
89: - Cloud session keeps working after you close your laptop
90: - Track progress from terminal or in the Devin web app
91: 
92: **Usage:**
93: 
94: ```bash
95: # Start a session, then hand off to cloud
96: devin -- "Fix the flaky integration tests in CI"
97: # Inside the REPL:
98: /handoff fix the flaky integration tests in CI
99: 
100: # Without a task description, continues from where you left off
101: /handoff
102: ```
103: 
104: **Best For:**
105: - Long-running tasks (migrations, batch jobs, large refactors)
106: - Browser-dependent workflows (OAuth flows, end-to-end tests, scraping)
107: - CI/CD pipeline debugging and deployments
108: - Parallel execution (offload to cloud while you keep coding locally)
109: 
110: Full handoff details: [cloud-handoff.md](./cloud-handoff.md)
111: 
112: ---
113: 
114: ### Multi-Model Selection
115: 
116: **Multiple AI models from multiple providers.** Devin CLI supports models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cognition, and leading open-source providers, with an intelligent Adaptive router.
117: 
118: **Capabilities:**
119: - Short names (`opus`, `sonnet`, `swe`, `gpt`, `codex`, `gemini`) resolve to latest versions
120: - `adaptive` mode auto-selects the best model per task
121: - Switch models mid-session with `/model <name>` slash command
122: - Configurable reasoning/thinking levels on supported models
123: - Cost optimization: use `swe` / `swe-1-6-fast` for cheap tasks, `opus` for deep reasoning
124: 
125: **Usage:**
126: 
127: ```bash
128: # Command flag
129: devin -p --model opus "Refactor the auth module"
130: devin -p --model swe-1-6-fast "Fix the typo at line 42"
131: 
132: # Slash command (inside REPL)
133: /model opus
134: /model codex
135: ```
136: 
137: **Best For:**
138: - Tasks that benefit from a specific provider's model
139: - Cost-sensitive workloads (SWE-1.6 for quick edits)
140: - Complex reasoning (Opus for architecture and security)
141: - Tasks where model diversity helps cross-validation
142: 
143: **Compared to other CLI executors:** Most CLI executors are locked to a single provider's models. Devin's multi-model surface lets the calling AI reach any provider through one binary.
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ### OS-Level Sandbox (--sandbox)
148: 
149: **Process sandboxing for autonomous execution.** The `--sandbox` flag enables OS-level sandboxing (macOS Seatbelt / Linux bwrap+seccomp) that enforces filesystem and network boundaries.
150: 
151: **Capabilities:**
152: - Shell commands and fetches auto-approve because the sandbox enforces what they can touch
153: - Direct file edits via `edit`/`write` tools still prompt (they run inside the CLI process, not the sandbox)
154: - Scopes granted mid-session dynamically expand the sandbox
155: - Domain allow/deny lists filter network access
156: - Only available with `autonomous` permission mode
157: 
158: **Usage:**
159: 
160: ```bash
161: # Autonomous mode with OS-enforced sandbox
162: devin --sandbox -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --model adaptive
163: ```
164: 
165: **Best For:**
166: - Unattended execution with OS-enforced safety limits
167: - Running untrusted or potentially destructive commands safely
168: - CI-like validation in an isolated environment
169: 
170: **Platform requirements:**
171: - macOS: works out of the box via Seatbelt
172: - Linux: requires `bwrap` and `socat` (run `devin sandbox setup` for prerequisites)
173: - Windows: use WSL 2 (native Windows cannot run the sandbox)
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 3. STANDARD TOOLS
178: 
179: These capabilities provide functionality comparable to other CLI executors, with Devin-specific syntax.
180: 
181: ### File System Operations
182: 
183: | Capability | Description | Devin Behavior |
184: |------------|-------------|----------------|
185: | File reading | Read file contents | Automatic or `@` file mention in REPL |
186: | File writing | Create or overwrite a file | Requires `accept-edits` or higher permission mode |
187: | Surgical edits | Replace text in a file | Automatic (targeted edits within files) |
188: | Multi-file read | Read multiple files | `@` mentions in REPL; file content piped via stdin in `-p` mode |
189: | Directory listing | List files and directories | Automatic pattern exploration |
190: | File search | Find files by pattern | `glob` tool |
191: | Content search | Search for text/regex in files | `grep` tool |
192: 
193: ### Shell Execution
194: 
195: | Capability | Description | Notes |
196: |------------|-------------|-------|
197: | Command execution | Run shell commands | `exec` tool; requires `accept-edits` or higher; auto-approved in `dangerous` or `autonomous` |
198: | Build and test | Run npm, cargo, pytest, etc. | Allowed at `accept-edits` and above |
199: | Git operations | git status, diff, add, commit | Allowed at `accept-edits` and above |
200: 
201: ### Web Access
202: 
203: | Capability | Description | Notes |
204: |------------|-------------|-------|
205: | URL fetching | Fetch web content | `fetch` tool; prompts in `auto`/`accept-edits`, auto in `dangerous`/`autonomous` |
206: | Web search | Search the web | Available through subagent tools and model capabilities |
207: 
208: ### Interaction
209: 
210: | Capability | Description | Notes |
211: |------------|-------------|-------|
212: | Clarification | Ask for input when needed | `ask_user_question` tool (not available to subagents) |
213: | Task tracking | Internal task management | Built into session context |
214: 
215: ---
216: 
217: ## 4. 4-TIER PERMISSION MODEL
218: 
219: Devin CLI uses a tiered permission system to balance power and safety. The `--permission-mode` flag controls which tools auto-approve and which prompt for approval.
220: 
221: ### Permission Modes
222: 
223: | Mode | Flag | Read-only | Fetch | Bash | File edits | When to use |
224: |------|------|-----------|-------|------|------------|-------------|
225: | **Auto** | `auto` | Auto | Prompt | Prompt | Prompt | Analysis, review, research |
226: | **Accept Edits** | `accept-edits` | Auto | Prompt | Prompt | Auto (workspace) | Code generation, refactoring |
227: | **Smart** | `smart` | Auto | Safe auto | Safe auto | Auto (workspace) | Trusted workflows with judgment |
228: | **Dangerous** | `dangerous` | Auto | Auto | Auto | Auto | Full trust — **explicit approval** |
229: | **Autonomous** | `autonomous` | Auto | Auto (sandbox) | Auto (sandbox) | Prompt | Unattended with `--sandbox` |
230: 
231: ### How Permissions Work
232: 
233: When the agent calls a tool, the permission system checks rules in priority order:
234: 
235: 1. **Deny rules** — Checked first. If matched, the action is blocked immediately.
236: 2. **Ask rules** — Checked second. If matched, always prompted (overrides allow rules).
237: 3. **Allow rules** — Checked last. If matched, the action proceeds without prompting.
238: 4. **Default** — If no rule matches, the behavior depends on the permission mode.
239: 
240: ### Permission Rule Syntax
241: 
242: **Scope-based:**
243: 
244: | Matcher | Controls | Example |
245: |---------|----------|---------|
246: | `Read(glob)` | File read access | `Read(src/**)` — all files under src/ |
247: | `Write(glob)` | File write access | `Write(src/**)` — write anywhere in src/ |
248: | `Exec(prefix)` | Shell command execution | `Exec(git)` — git, git status, git commit... |
249: | `Fetch(pattern)` | HTTP fetch access | `Fetch(https://api.github.com/*)` |
250: 
251: **Tool-based:** `read`, `edit`, `grep`, `glob`, `exec`
252: 
253: **MCP tool-based:** `mcp__server__tool`, `mcp__server__*`, `mcp__*`
254: 
255: ### Permission Precedence
256: 
257: 1. Organization/team settings (if enterprise) — highest
258: 2. Session-level grants (interactive approvals)
259: 3. Project local config (`.devin/config.local.json`)
260: 4. Project config (`.devin/config.json`)
261: 5. User config (`~/.config/devin/config.json`) — lowest
262: 
263: Deny is checked before ask, and ask before allow. A deny rule always wins. Organization-level denials cannot be overridden.
264: 
265: ### Bypass vs Autonomous
266: 
267: | | Bypass (`dangerous`) | Autonomous (`--sandbox`) |
268: |---|---|---|
269: | Requires `--sandbox` | No | Yes (only mode available in sandbox) |
270: | Shell commands | Auto-approved, unrestricted | Auto-approved, contained by sandbox |
271: | File writes via edit/write | Auto-approved anywhere | Still prompt (granting scope expands sandbox) |
272: | Network access | Unrestricted | Filtered by sandbox domain lists |
273: | Respects admin Team Settings | Yes | Yes |
274: 
275: Pick `dangerous` when you trust the agent with your whole machine. Pick `--sandbox` (autonomous) when you want unattended execution with OS-enforced limits.
276: 
277: ---
278: 
279: ## 5. MCP SERVER INTEGRATION (devin mcp)
280: 
281: **Model Context Protocol server support.** Devin CLI connects to MCP servers, extending its capabilities with custom tools and data sources.
282: 
283: **Subcommands:**
284: 
285: | Command | Description |
286: |---------|-------------|
287: | `devin mcp add <name>` | Add a new MCP server (stdio or HTTP transport) |
288: | `devin mcp list` | List all configured MCP servers |
289: | `devin mcp get <name>` | Show details for a specific server |
290: | `devin mcp remove <name>` | Remove a configured server |
291: | `devin mcp login <name>` | Authenticate with a server via OAuth |
292: | `devin mcp logout <name>` | Remove stored OAuth credentials |
293: | `devin mcp enable <name>` | Enable a disabled server |
294: | `devin mcp disable <name>` | Disable a server without removing it |
295: 
296: **Configuration:**
297: 
298: ```json
299: // .devin/config.json
300: {
301:   "mcpServers": {
302:     "my-server": {
303:       "command": "node",
304:       "args": ["./mcp-server.js"],
305:       "env": {
306:         "MY_API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}"
307:       },
308:       "transport": "stdio"
309:     }
310:   }
311: }
312: ```
313: 
314: **Usage examples:**
315: 
316: ```bash
317: # stdio server
318: devin mcp add my-server -- npx @company/mcp-server --port 3000
319: 
320: # HTTP server
321: devin mcp add notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
322: 
323: # With environment variables
324: devin mcp add -e GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxx github -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github
325: 
326: # Use MCP tools in a dispatch
327: devin -p "Use the database MCP tool to query user records" \
328:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto
329: ```
330: 
331: **MCP tool permissions:** Control access with `mcp__server__tool`, `mcp__server__*`, or `mcp__*` patterns in the permissions config.
332: 
333: ---
334: 
335: ## 6. SESSION MANAGEMENT
336: 
337: **Multi-turn workflow continuity.** Devin CLI supports continuing and resuming sessions, forking, and reverting.
338: 
339: **Capabilities:**
340: - `devin -c` / `--continue` — Continue the most recent session in the current directory
341: - `devin -r <id>` / `--resume <id>` — Resume a specific session by ID
342: - `/fork [step]` — Fork the current session to explore alternatives
343: - `/revert <step>` — Revert file changes from a specific step and rewind conversation
344: - `/ls [--all]` — List recent sessions
345: - `devin list --format json` — Scripted session listing
346: - Sessions persist conversation context across invocations
347: 
348: **Usage:**
349: 
350: ```bash
351: # Continue most recent session
352: devin -c
353: 
354: # Resume specific session
355: devin -r brisk-otter
356: 
357: # Non-interactive continuation
358: devin -c -p "Continue implementing the rate limiter" --model adaptive
359: 
360: # List sessions as JSON
361: devin list --format json
362: ```
363: 
364: **Compared to other CLI executors:** Session continuity with full conversation and tool-call context preservation. Fork and revert provide safe exploration of alternatives.
365: 
366: ---
367: 
368: ## 7. CAPABILITY COMPARISON
369: 
370: | Capability | Calling AI | Devin CLI | Notes |
371: |------------|-------------|-----------|-------|
372: | **File reading** | `Read` tool | `read` tool, `@` mentions | Devin `@` syntax is concise |
373: | **File writing** | `Write`, `Edit` | `edit`, `write` tools | Requires `accept-edits` or higher |
374: | **Code search** | `Grep` (ripgrep) | `grep` tool | Both ripgrep-powered |
375: | **File discovery** | `Glob` | `glob` tool | Functionally equivalent |
376: | **Shell commands** | `Bash` | `exec` tool | Both require appropriate permissions |
377: | **Web fetch** | `WebFetch` | `fetch` tool (the hook payload names it `webfetch`) | Similar capabilities |
378: | **Subagent delegation** | Not native | `run_subagent` tool | Devin-exclusive native subagents |
379: | **Cloud handoff** | Not built-in | `/handoff` command | Devin-exclusive |
380: | **Multi-model** | Single model | Multiple providers | Devin supports Opus, Sonnet, GPT, SWE, Codex, Gemini, etc. |
381: | **OS-level sandbox** | Not built-in | `--sandbox` flag | Devin-exclusive |
382: | **Session continuity** | Built-in (conversation) | `-c`, `-r`, `/fork`, `/revert` | Devin preserves full context |
383: | **MCP integration** | Native | `devin mcp` subcommands | Both support MCP protocol |
384: | **Memory/persistence** | Spec-folder continuity docs | Session resume/fork | Different approaches |
385: | **Image input** | `Read` (multimodal) | Clipboard paste (`Ctrl+V`) | Both support image input |
386: 
387: ---
388: 
389: ## 8. BEST PRACTICES
390: 
391: ### When to Use run_subagent
392: 
393: - Parallel research across multiple independent modules
394: - Cost-effective exploration (explore subagent on SWE-1.6)
395: - Isolating subtask context from the parent conversation
396: - Code changes that benefit from focused, independent work
397: 
398: **Avoid for:** Tasks that share context with the parent or need the parent's full conversation history.
399: 
400: ### When to Use /handoff
401: 
402: - Long-running tasks that exceed local session time
403: - Browser-dependent workflows (OAuth, E2E tests, scraping)
404: - CI/CD pipeline debugging and deployments
405: - Parallel execution (offload to cloud while you keep coding locally)
406: 
407: **Avoid for:** Quick edits that complete faster locally; tasks involving sensitive data without confirming cloud isolation.
408: 
409: ### When to Use Multi-Model
410: 
411: - `adaptive` for general delegation (router picks the best model)
412: - `opus` for complex refactoring, architecture, security
413: - `swe-1-6-fast` for quick edits and cost-sensitive work
414: - `gpt` / `codex` when OpenAI-model strengths fit the task
415: 
416: **Avoid for:** Tasks where a single model already handles well and switching adds overhead.
417: 
418: ### When to Use --sandbox
419: 
420: - Unattended execution with OS-enforced safety limits
421: - Running potentially destructive commands safely
422: - CI-like validation in an isolated environment
423: 
424: **Avoid for:** Interactive sessions where you want to approve actions; tasks needing unrestricted network access.
425: 
426: ### Permission Mode Selection Patterns
427: 
428: | Use Case | Permission Mode | Rationale |
429: |----------|----------------|-----------|
430: | Code review | `auto` | Prevent accidental modifications |
431: | Security audit | `auto` | Strict isolation for safety analysis |
432: | Research | `auto` | No file system changes needed |
433: | Code generation | `accept-edits` | Files must be created |
434: | Bug fixing | `accept-edits` | Files must be modified |
435: | Test generation | `accept-edits` | Test files must be written |
436: | Documentation | `accept-edits` | Docs must be written |
437: | Unattended execution | `autonomous` (+ `--sandbox`) | OS-enforced safety |
438: | Full trust | `dangerous` | **Ask user first** |
439: 
440: ### Capability Combination Patterns
441: 
442: | Goal | Capability Combination | Flow |
443: |------|----------------------|------|
444: | **Understand then fix** | `auto` analysis → `accept-edits` fix | Analyze, focus, edit |
445: | **Parallel research** | `run_subagent` with explore subagents | Spawn, wait, synthesize |
446: | **Offload long task** | `/handoff` to cloud | Start locally, hand off, track remotely |
447: | **Audit codebase** | `auto` analysis with `opus` | Deep read-only review |
448: | **Multi-session task** | Initial `-p` → `-c` continue → `/fork` alternatives | Start, continue, branch |
449: | **Safe unattended** | `--sandbox` autonomous | OS-enforced limits |

217: ## 4. 4-TIER PERMISSION MODEL
218: 
219: Devin CLI uses a tiered permission system to balance power and safety. The `--permission-mode` flag controls which tools auto-approve and which prompt for approval.
220: 
221: ### Permission Modes
222: 
223: | Mode | Flag | Read-only | Fetch | Bash | File edits | When to use |
224: |------|------|-----------|-------|------|------------|-------------|
225: | **Auto** | `auto` | Auto | Prompt | Prompt | Prompt | Analysis, review, research |
226: | **Accept Edits** | `accept-edits` | Auto | Prompt | Prompt | Auto (workspace) | Code generation, refactoring |
227: | **Smart** | `smart` | Auto | Safe auto | Safe auto | Auto (workspace) | Trusted workflows with judgment |
228: | **Dangerous** | `dangerous` | Auto | Auto | Auto | Auto | Full trust — **explicit approval** |
229: | **Autonomous** | `autonomous` | Auto | Auto (sandbox) | Auto (sandbox) | Prompt | Unattended with `--sandbox` |
230: 
231: ### How Permissions Work
232: 
233: When the agent calls a tool, the permission system checks rules in priority order:
234: 
235: 1. **Deny rules** — Checked first. If matched, the action is blocked immediately.
236: 2. **Ask rules** — Checked second. If matched, always prompted (overrides allow rules).
237: 3. **Allow rules** — Checked last. If matched, the action proceeds without prompting.
238: 4. **Default** — If no rule matches, the behavior depends on the permission mode.
239: 
240: ### Permission Rule Syntax
241: 
242: **Scope-based:**
243: 
244: | Matcher | Controls | Example |
245: |---------|----------|---------|
246: | `Read(glob)` | File read access | `Read(src/**)` — all files under src/ |
247: | `Write(glob)` | File write access | `Write(src/**)` — write anywhere in src/ |
248: | `Exec(prefix)` | Shell command execution | `Exec(git)` — git, git status, git commit... |
249: | `Fetch(pattern)` | HTTP fetch access | `Fetch(https://api.github.com/*)` |
250: 
251: **Tool-based:** `read`, `edit`, `grep`, `glob`, `exec`
252: 
253: **MCP tool-based:** `mcp__server__tool`, `mcp__server__*`, `mcp__*`
254: 
255: ### Permission Precedence
256: 
257: 1. Organization/team settings (if enterprise) — highest
258: 2. Session-level grants (interactive approvals)
259: 3. Project local config (`.devin/config.local.json`)
260: 4. Project config (`.devin/config.json`)
261: 5. User config (`~/.config/devin/config.json`) — lowest
262: 
263: Deny is checked before ask, and ask before allow. A deny rule always wins. Organization-level denials cannot be overridden.
264: 
265: ### Bypass vs Autonomous
266: 
267: | | Bypass (`dangerous`) | Autonomous (`--sandbox`) |
268: |---|---|---|
269: | Requires `--sandbox` | No | Yes (only mode available in sandbox) |
270: | Shell commands | Auto-approved, unrestricted | Auto-approved, contained by sandbox |
271: | File writes via edit/write | Auto-approved anywhere | Still prompt (granting scope expands sandbox) |
272: | Network access | Unrestricted | Filtered by sandbox domain lists |
273: | Respects admin Team Settings | Yes | Yes |
274: 
275: Pick `dangerous` when you trust the agent with your whole machine. Pick `--sandbox` (autonomous) when you want unattended execution with OS-enforced limits.
276:

279: ## 5. MCP SERVER INTEGRATION (devin mcp)
280: 
281: **Model Context Protocol server support.** Devin CLI connects to MCP servers, extending its capabilities with custom tools and data sources.
282: 
283: **Subcommands:**
284: 
285: | Command | Description |
286: |---------|-------------|
287: | `devin mcp add <name>` | Add a new MCP server (stdio or HTTP transport) |
288: | `devin mcp list` | List all configured MCP servers |
289: | `devin mcp get <name>` | Show details for a specific server |
290: | `devin mcp remove <name>` | Remove a configured server |
291: | `devin mcp login <name>` | Authenticate with a server via OAuth |
292: | `devin mcp logout <name>` | Remove stored OAuth credentials |
293: | `devin mcp enable <name>` | Enable a disabled server |
294: | `devin mcp disable <name>` | Disable a server without removing it |
295: 
296: **Configuration:**
297: 
298: ```json
299: // .devin/config.json
300: {
301:   "mcpServers": {
302:     "my-server": {
303:       "command": "node",
304:       "args": ["./mcp-server.js"],
305:       "env": {
306:         "MY_API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}"
307:       },
308:       "transport": "stdio"
309:     }
310:   }
311: }
312: ```
313: 
314: **Usage examples:**
315: 
316: ```bash

318: devin mcp add my-server -- npx @company/mcp-server --port 3000
319: 
320: # HTTP server

322: 
323: # With environment variables

325: 
326: # Use MCP tools in a dispatch
327: devin -p "Use the database MCP tool to query user records" \
328:   --model adaptive --permission-mode auto
329: ```

331: **MCP tool permissions:** Control access with `mcp__server__tool`, `mcp__server__*`, or `mcp__*` patterns in the permissions config.

335: ## 6. SESSION MANAGEMENT
336: 
337: **Multi-turn workflow continuity.** Devin CLI supports continuing and resuming sessions, forking, and reverting.
338: 
339: **Capabilities:**
340: - `devin -c` / `--continue` — Continue the most recent session in the current directory
341: - `devin -r <id>` / `--resume <id>` — Resume a specific session by ID
342: - `/fork [step]` — Fork the current session to explore alternatives
343: - `/revert <step>` — Revert file changes from a specific step and rewind conversation
344: - `/ls [--all]` — List recent sessions
345: - `devin list --format json` — Scripted session listing
346: - Sessions persist conversation context across invocations
347: 
348: **Usage:**
349: 
350: ```bash
351: # Continue most recent session
352: devin -c
353: 
354: # Resume specific session
355: devin -r brisk-otter
356: 
357: # Non-interactive continuation
358: devin -c -p "Continue implementing the rate limiter" --model adaptive
359: 
360: # List sessions as JSON
361: devin list --format json
362: ```
363: 
364: **Compared to other CLI executors:** Session continuity with full conversation and tool-call context preservation. Fork and revert provide safe exploration of alternatives.
365:

389: ## 8. BEST PRACTICES
390: 
391: ### When to Use run_subagent
392: 
393: - Parallel research across multiple independent modules
394: - Cost-effective exploration (explore subagent on SWE-1.6)
395: - Isolating subtask context from the parent conversation
396: - Code changes that benefit from focused, independent work
397: 
398: **Avoid for:** Tasks that share context with the parent or need the parent's full conversation history.
399: 
400: ### When to Use /handoff
401: 
402: - Long-running tasks that exceed local session time
403: - Browser-dependent workflows (OAuth, E2E tests, scraping)
404: - CI/CD pipeline debugging and deployments
405: - Parallel execution (offload to cloud while you keep coding locally)
406: 
407: **Avoid for:** Quick edits that complete faster locally; tasks involving sensitive data without confirming cloud isolation.
408: 
409: ### When to Use Multi-Model
410: 
411: - `adaptive` for general delegation (router picks the best model)
412: - `opus` for complex refactoring, architecture, security
413: - `swe-1-6-fast` for quick edits and cost-sensitive work
414: - `gpt` / `codex` when OpenAI-model strengths fit the task
415: 
416: **Avoid for:** Tasks where a single model already handles well and switching adds overhead.
417: 
418: ### When to Use --sandbox
419: 
420: - Unattended execution with OS-enforced safety limits
421: - Running potentially destructive commands safely
422: - CI-like validation in an isolated environment
423: 
424: **Avoid for:** Interactive sessions where you want to approve actions; tasks needing unrestricted network access.
425: 
426: ### Permission Mode Selection Patterns
427: 
428: | Use Case | Permission Mode | Rationale |
429: |----------|----------------|-----------|
430: | Code review | `auto` | Prevent accidental modifications |
431: | Security audit | `auto` | Strict isolation for safety analysis |
432: | Research | `auto` | No file system changes needed |
433: | Code generation | `accept-edits` | Files must be created |
434: | Bug fixing | `accept-edits` | Files must be modified |
435: | Test generation | `accept-edits` | Test files must be written |
436: | Documentation | `accept-edits` | Docs must be written |
437: | Unattended execution | `autonomous` (+ `--sandbox`) | OS-enforced safety |
438: | Full trust | `dangerous` | **Ask user first** |
439: 
440: ### Capability Combination Patterns
441: 
442: | Goal | Capability Combination | Flow |
443: |------|----------------------|------|
444: | **Understand then fix** | `auto` analysis → `accept-edits` fix | Analyze, focus, edit |
445: | **Parallel research** | `run_subagent` with explore subagents | Spawn, wait, synthesize |
446: | **Offload long task** | `/handoff` to cloud | Start locally, hand off, track remotely |
447: | **Audit codebase** | `auto` analysis with `opus` | Deep read-only review |
448: | **Multi-session task** | Initial `-p` → `-c` continue → `/fork` alternatives | Start, continue, branch |
